subject: stick insect
title: Birds Eat Stick Insect Eggs. Up to 1 in 5 Comes Out Intact

scenes.text: Getting eaten by a bird may be how this insect travels.
Stick insects are slow, and many can't fly. Yet relatives reach faraway islands.
Scientists in Japan fed their eggs to brown-eared bulbuls, birds that hunt them.
In one test, fourteen of seventy eggs came out intact. Two hatched.
The shell is hard like a seed, coated in crystals that resist digestion.
So a bird that eats a female full of eggs may carry her babies far away.

description:
Japanese researchers fed stick insect eggs to brown-eared bulbuls, one of their main predators. Depending on the species, 5 to 20 percent passed through the birds intact.
In one test 14 of 70 eggs survived and two hatched. The hard, seed-like eggs may let flightless stick insects spread the way plants do, inside birds. The study was published in Ecology.
Would you call that surviving or hitchhiking?
thumbnail_text: EATEN BY A BIRD. THEN HATCHED.
first_comment: Plants have done this for millions of years: fruit gets eaten, seeds come out somewhere new. Stick insect eggs even look like seeds. What other animal do you think could pull this off?
